title: A Dynamical Mechanism for Irreversibility in Cyclically Driven Amorphous Solids
authors: Sauvik Chatterjee, Asaf Szulc, Ido Regev
abstract: Amorphous solids subjected to athermal quasistatic oscillatory shear undergo a transition from periodic reversible dynamics to irreversible diffusive dynamics at yielding. How irreversibility arises in such deterministic, dissipative dynamics remains unclear. Here we show that trajectories remain locally stable, with perturbations decaying rather than growing even in the irreversible regime, ruling out the sustained exponential sensitivity to initial conditions associated with chaotic dynamics. Rather than diverging continuously, nearby trajectories initially remain close before eventually separating through rare branching events, after which their separation grows diffusively. A mean-field soft-spot model reproduces the same branching statistics and reveals their microscopic origin. We find that branching originates from competition between nearly-degenerate plastic instabilities, in which a small perturbation changes which instability activates first and thereby alters the subsequent sequence of plastic events. These results identify instability-selection-induced branching as a dynamical mechanism for irreversibility in cyclically driven amorphous solids.
summary: This work identifies 'instability-selection-induced branching' as the dynamical source of irreversibility in amorphous solids when they yield under cyclic stress. By comparing particle simulations to a soft-spot model, the authors rule out chaos and demonstrate that the system's path dependence is governed by rare events where competing plastic instabilities dictate the sequence of subsequent structural rearrangements.
main_problem: The study addresses the fundamental dynamical mechanism responsible for irreversibility when amorphous solids transition from reversible periodic dynamics to irreversible diffusive dynamics upon yielding under cyclic shear.
main_result: Irreversibility is shown to arise not from chaotic sensitivity to initial conditions, but from 'instability-selection-induced branching' events occurring during plastic activity.
method: The authors employed both particle-based simulations (Kob-Andersen model) and a coarse-grained mean-field soft-spot model to analyze trajectory separation dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is amorphous solids subjected to athermal quasistatic oscillatory shear. The theoretical framework utilizes a soft-spot model where plasticity is governed by the competition between nearly-degenerate local instabilities (soft spots).
key_observables: Trajectory separation distance ($D_r(n)$), waiting-time distributions for branching events, and Mean Square Displacement ($\Delta R_n$) scaling.
important_parameters: Critical strain amplitude ($\gamma_{	ext{max}}$) marking the yield transition; perturbation size ($\delta$); soft spot thresholds ($\sigma+_n, \sigma-_n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that trajectory separation after branching follows diffusive scaling, and that waiting times between plastic events can be modeled by an exponential distribution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decay of perturbations (ruling out chaos), the clear onset of irreversible dynamics via persistent trajectory branching, and the linear scaling ($\propto n$) of Mean Square Displacement confirming diffusion after these branching events.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes that standard chaotic diagnostics fail to explain irreversibility. It then introduces the soft-spot model to show how competition between instabilities causes stochastic 'branching' in the configuration space, which is identified as the source of irreversible dynamics, followed by confirmation using diffusive scaling measurements.
why_interesting: While focused on classical amorphous solids, the concept of instability selection leading to non-equilibrium path dependence (memory/hysteresis) has parallels in understanding decoherence or dissipation mechanisms in open quantum systems where system evolution is constrained by local minima or metastable states.

FIG. 4. An example of the beginning of a trajectory branching observed in the soft-spot model. The reference and perturbed trajectories visit the same sequence of configurations up to state C. At state C, a small perturbation reverses the ordering of two competing instabilities. In the reference trajectory, soft spot 667 at site 157 is activated first, whereas in the perturbed trajectory soft spot 863 at site 187 is activated first. This difference modifies the subsequent stress redistribution and results in different sequences of plastic events and sustained trajectory separation.

FIG. 5. (a) Distances to instability xi = σ+ i −σi for state C, immediately before the branching event. Sites 157 and 187, marked by the arrows, are the only sites with negative values of xi and form a nearly-degenerate pair of competing insta- bilities. (b) Competition variable ∆= x187 −x157. In the reference trajectory ∆> 0, indicating that site 157 is more unstable and is therefore activated first. In the perturbed tra- jectory ∆< 0, indicating that site 187 is activated first. The perturbation therefore changes the ordering of the competing instabilities and initiates trajectory branching.
